entries.english: Turkana Life-Stages (Nidue/Egile/Kasikou & Apesur/Aberu/Agemat), Warrior Ages (Asavanissia), Oppa Elders, Deities (Agipie) & Marriage Law (Dundas 1910, pp. 67–69)
entries.translation: Male & Female Life-Stages (p. 67): Male: (1) nidue (young boy), (2) egile (warrior), (3) kasikou (old man; titled oppa and entitled to wear a beaded head-dress); Female: (1) apesur (girl), (2) aberu (married woman), (3) agemat (old woman) • Warrior Generations: asavanissia (a new warrior age-set created every 4–5 years; vigorous non-drinking elders form the first line of village defence, subsisting on camel milk and Nessegonn bushes) • Dual Deities (p. 69): Agipie (benevolent sky god) vs. the malevolent Nether-World God dwelling in rocks, mountains, rivers, and underground (where cattle, sheep, goats, and talking people live; thunderstorms are the two gods fighting and hurling lightning) • Bride-Price & Post-Marriage Mock-Assault Feast (p. 68): 20 cattle + 30 donkeys to the bride's mother before marriage, 30 cattle + camels/donkeys/sheep/goats to the father, 5 cattle to each co-wife, and 2 cattle to each sibling (or 30 cattle fine per lover for premarital pregnancy); a married daughter may not enter her father's kraal until he slaughters 2 bullocks in a special enclosure stormed by singing guests imitating an attack on an enemy kraal

entries.english: Sir Harry Johnston's (1902, Vol. II, pp. 839–852) Ethnography of the Turkana: Stature, Felted Hair-Bags, Circular Wrist-Knife, Ostrich-Egg Aprons, Dūm-Palm Meal & Elephant Snares
entries.translation: Physical stature & coiffure (pp. 841–846): tallest people on the globe (Capt. Wellby noted districts averaging ~7 ft); men train their hair with fat, clay, and inherited paternal felt into huge back-bags (chignons) holding fire-sticks, snuff, and beads, or into long pendulous pods terminating in a wire tail, topped by felted human-hair hats sewn with cowries and brass beads or black ostrich-feather caps; women do not shave their heads (unlike Suk and Masai women), twisting their hair into bast-stiffened tails • Ornaments & weapons (pp. 844–850): 2 to 8 brass/iron rings along the outer ear-rim, nose-septum flat brass disc, lower-lip quill, circular steel wrist-knife (sharpened on outer edge, sheathed in leather), right-arm leather band with white cow-tail or colobus tassel, 6-inch-backed brass-beaded goatskin waist-belt, girls' aprons edged with ostrich-egg shell discs, antelope knuckle-bone necklaces, Beisa oryx-horn tobacco boxes, tiny 8-inch carved 3-legged stools/headrests, and concave-sided 4-pointed buffalo/giraffe-hide shields with a bow-shaped wooden midrib topped by a feather plume • Subsistence & elephant snares (pp. 848–850): meal ground from the gingerbread-like rind of Dūm palm (Hyphæne thebaica) fruits, fishing in Lake Rudolf, humped cattle, black-headed sheep, donkeys, and camels (acquired via Burkeneji); catching elephants with raw-hide running nooses anchored to big river-valley trees over muddy watering paths • Language note (p. 887): Turkana uses the negative prefix Nye- (unlike Ma- in Masai/Suk) and masculine e-/l- vs. feminine a-/n-/nya- gender prefixes (p. 910 fn.)

entries.translation: Recorded by a native clerk from the CMS Mission at Taveta for Sir Charles Eliot (Hollis 1909, pp. xxix–xxxiii): Gender & Demonstrative Prefixes: Masculine e- / lo- (pl. ngi- / lu-), Feminine a- / na- (pl. nga- / nu-), Neuter/Diminutive i- / yeni- (pl. ngi-) • Personal Pronouns (p. xxxi): aiyong (I), iyong (thou), ngesi (he/she), suwa (we), eesi (ye), kesi (they) • Cardinal Numerals 1–10 (p. xxx): 1 epei, 2 ngarei, 3 ngauni, 4 ngomwon, 5 ngakan, 6 ngakan-k-apei, 7 ngakan-ka-ngarei, 8 ngakan-ka-ngauni, 9 ngakan-ka-ngomwon, 10 ngatomon • Comparative Nouns & Verbs (pp. xxx–xxxiii): akuj (God/up), akolong (sun), elap (moon), ngakipi (water), akim (fire), etunganan (man, pl. ngitunga), aberu (woman, pl. ngaberu), ikoku (child, pl. ngidwe), aite (cow, pl. ngatuk), akine (goat, pl. ngakinei), emesek (sheep, pl. ngimesekin), eingok (dog, pl. ngiingokwo), akwara (spear), ekipire (feather), a-los-it (to go), a-bun-ere (to come), a-nyam (to eat), a-mat (to drink), a-per (to sleep), a-mina (to love)
entries.pronunciation: ai-yong, i-yong, nge-si, su-wa, ee-si, ke-si • e-pei, nga-rei, nga-u-ni, ngo-mwon, nga-kan, nga-to-mon
entries.context: Sir Charles Eliot in A. C. Hollis (1909) 'The Nandi: Their Language and Folk-Lore', Introduction pp. xxix–xxxiii

entries.english: Turkana Dual Leadership (Lemurok Hereditary Seers & Lekatuknok Advisers), Customary Law & Turkana–Suk Comparative Table (Beech 1911, pp. 27–37, 150–151)
entries.translation: Recorded from Chief Aijigwa of Naudu and Salali & Hon. A. Bruce (Beech 1911, pp. 27–37, 150–151): Dual Leadership (pp. 36–37): (1) Lemurok (hereditary wizard-chiefs, only two in the whole tribe, whose magic is required before war or moving cattle to new pastures to detect tsetse fly and cattle disease) and (2) Lekatuknok (sectional advisers) • Customary Law (pp. 28–35): Oath by stepping over two spears point-to-point; Grave Offence punished by spearing and confiscation of all property except donkeys (believed to cause the receiver's death); Theft = return of goods on 1st offence, + 1 bullock on 2nd offence; Slander = 1 bullock fine; Bride-price = minimum 5 cattle + 100 sheep; Beggars employed as herders and allowed to acquire stock; Eldest son inherits most of father's property and father's wives • Turkana–Suk Comparative Vocabulary (pp. 150–151): nya-tapor (pl. ñga-taparin, pond), nye-yokon (herdsman), nye-kitoi (pl. ñgi-kito, tree), nye-sikirya (donkey), nya-o (pl. ñga-awa, bee), ñga-kile (milk), nya-muro (pl. ñga-mur, cooking-pot stones), nye-doket (pl. ñgi-doketa, ford), nya-peryet (bed), nye-kori (giraffe), nye-ñgole (horse), apuru (smoke), edoñga (song), akholopoch (spoon), nya-khai (house), nya-rug (hump), nya-khamir (hunger), ekhol-a (fish), asepich (detachment), ekuryana (coward), ñgi-cholongo (chair), akhoit (pl. nya-koyo, bone), ñga-sowa (buffaloes), etyañg (animal), ekwaye (river bank), em-baso (lake, p. 137)
entries.context: Mervyn W. H. Beech (1911) 'The Suk: Their Language and Folklore', Chapter II pp. 27–37 & Appendix pp. 150–151
